safe-sandbox.question: In a sandbox whose global configuration file is empty, you run git -c user.name=Fixture commit. What does git config --global user.name print afterwards?
options: Nothing; the -c value applied only to that one command
Fixture
The author name of the last commit
safe-sandbox.explanation: A -c value overrides configuration for a single invocation and is never written to a file. The global scope stays as it was, which is why the sandbox can commit without touching your identity.

three-states.question: notes.txt is committed as "one". You change it to "two" and stage it, then change it to "three" without staging. What does plain git diff show?
options: The change from two to three
The change from one to two
The change from one to three
three-states.explanation: Plain git diff compares the working tree with the index. The index holds the staged "two", so only the later, unstaged edit appears.

inspect-changes.question: One file is staged and another is modified but not staged. Which command lists only the staged file's name?
options: git diff --cached --name-only
git diff --name-only
git status --ignored
inspect-changes.explanation: --cached compares the index with HEAD, and --name-only prints file names. Plain git diff --name-only lists the unstaged file instead.

coherent-commits.question: parser.py is staged and notes.txt is modified but not staged. After git commit -m "Add parser", what does git status --short show for notes.txt?
options: M notes.txt: modified, still not staged
M  notes.txt: staged for the next commit
Nothing: it was committed too
coherent-commits.explanation: A commit records the index only. notes.txt keeps its unstaged edit, shown with M in the second column.

ignore-secrets.question: local.env is listed in .gitignore and has never been tracked. What does git status --short show after you edit it?
options: Nothing for local.env
?? local.env
M local.env
ignore-secrets.explanation: An ignored, untracked file is left out of status. git check-ignore -v local.env shows which rule ignores it.

history-refs.question: How many parents does the commit created by git merge --no-ff topic have?
history-refs.explanation: A merge commit records both histories it joins: the previous tip of the current branch and the tip of topic. git log --pretty=%P -n 1 lists them.

branch-switch.question: On main you run git switch -c feature and make no commits. Which commit does feature point to?
options: The same commit as main
A new empty commit
The first commit in the repository
branch-switch.explanation: Creating a branch adds a reference to the current commit. It copies no files and creates no commit until you commit on it.

restore-staging.question: notes.txt has an unstaged edit. What does git restore -- notes.txt, without --staged, do?
options: Discards the edit, restoring the file from the index
Unstages the file and keeps the edit
Creates a commit that undoes the edit
restore-staging.explanation: Without --staged, restore rewrites the working file from the index, so the unstaged edit is lost. Copy anything you might need first.

merge-integration.question: main has not moved since topic branched from it. What does git merge topic do by default?
options: Moves main forward to topic's commit, with no merge commit
Creates a merge commit with two parents
Refuses until you add --no-ff
merge-integration.explanation: When the current branch is an ancestor of topic, Git fast-forwards: main simply moves to topic's commit. --no-ff forces a merge commit instead.

conflict-resolution.question: A merge stops with a conflict in config.txt. What does git status --short show for that file?
options: UU config.txt
M  config.txt
?? config.txt
conflict-resolution.explanation: UU means both sides changed the file and the conflict is unresolved. After you edit and stage the resolution, it shows as an ordinary staged change.

remotes-fetch.question: After git fetch, origin/main has 2 commits that your main lacks, and main has none of its own. What does git status report?
options: Behind origin/main by 2 commits and can be fast-forwarded
Up to date with origin/main
Diverged from origin/main
remotes-fetch.explanation: Fetch updated origin/main but not your branch. Status compares the two and says you are behind; git merge --ff-only or git pull integrates them.

pull-request-review.question: After feature branched, main gained a commit that changes other.txt. What does git diff main...feature (three dots) show?
options: Only feature's changes since the common ancestor
feature's changes plus the reversal of main's new commit
Only main's new commit
pull-request-review.explanation: Three dots diff from the merge base to feature, which is what a reviewer of feature needs. Two dots would compare the two tips and show main's change as if feature removed it.

branching-strategies.question: A product supports versions 3.1 and 3.2 while developing 3.3 on main. A security fix is needed in all three. Where should it land first?
options: On the oldest release branch, then merged forward
On main, then cherry-picked to release/3.2 and release/3.1
Only on release/3.2, since that is the newest release
branching-strategies.explanation: Fixing main first guarantees the next release includes it; backports to supported release branches follow with cherry-pick -x for traceability.

revert-reset.question: HEAD added the line "beta" to notes.txt. What does git revert HEAD produce?
options: A new commit that removes the line; the original stays in history
The branch moves back one commit and the original disappears
An unstaged edit that removes the line
revert-reset.explanation: Revert records a compensating commit on top. History gains a commit rather than losing one, which is why it suits shared branches.

reflog-recovery.question: You run git reset --hard HEAD~1 by mistake. Which reference names the commit you just left?
options: HEAD@{1}
HEAD~1
ORIG_MAIN
reflog-recovery.explanation: The reflog records where HEAD pointed before each move, so HEAD@{1} is the previous position. HEAD~1 is now the parent of the new HEAD.

bisect.question: git bisect starts with 16 commits after the known good one, the last of them known bad. Git checks out a midpoint and prints "Bisecting: 7 revisions left to test after this (roughly K steps)". What is K?
bisect.explanation: The first midpoint already halves the 16 candidates, so about 8 remain and log2(8) = 3 more tests find the first bad commit: about log2(16) = 4 tests in all.

investigate-history.question: client.py was renamed to http_client.py two commits ago. What does `git log --format=%s -- http_client.py` list?
options: Every commit in the file's history
Only the commits since the rename; --follow continues past it
Nothing until the rename is committed again
investigate-history.explanation: Path filtering uses the current name, so the log stops at the rename commit. --follow tracks one file through renames.

cherry-pick.question: What does git cherry-pick -x C add to the new commit's message?
options: A line naming C: (cherry picked from commit followed by C's ID)
Nothing; -x only checks for conflicts
C's author name in place of yours
cherry-pick.explanation: -x appends a reference to the original commit, so a maintenance branch records where the fix came from.

rebase.question: topic has 3 commits that main lacks. After git rebase main, how many commits does git rev-list --count main..topic report?
options: 3, each with a new ID
1, the commits squashed
0, the commits moved into main
rebase.explanation: Rebase replays each commit onto main's tip. The topic keeps three commits, but their parents change, so their IDs change. main itself does not move.

interactive-rebase.question: A branch has "Add CSV parser", "Add parser tests" and "fixup! Add CSV parser". After git rebase -i --autosquash main with the list accepted, how many commits are on the branch?
interactive-rebase.explanation: Autosquash moves the fixup under its target and marks it fixup, so it melds into Add CSV parser, leaving two commits.

stash.question: notes.txt is tracked and modified. After git stash, what does git status --short show?
options: Nothing: the working tree matches HEAD
M notes.txt
?? notes.txt
stash.explanation: An ordinary stash saves tracked changes and resets them to HEAD. git stash pop reapplies them.

tags-release.question: You tag a commit v1.0 with git tag -a, then make one more commit. What does git describe print?
options: v1.0-1-g followed by the short commit ID
tags-release.explanation: describe names the nearest annotated tag, the number of commits since it, and g plus the abbreviated ID of the current commit.

repository-configuration.question: A pre-commit hook exits with status 1. What happens to the commit?
options: It is created, and the hook's message is shown as a warning
No commit is created; the staged changes remain staged
The staged changes are discarded
repository-configuration.explanation: A non-zero exit from pre-commit aborts the commit before it is recorded. The index is left as it was.

team-release-review.question: A release fails after deployment. Which step does the course's workflow take before choosing a revert or a forward fix?
options: Preserve evidence and stop the harmful rollout
Force-push main back to the previous tag
Delete the release tag
team-release-review.explanation: The lesson's recovery order is to preserve evidence, stop harmful rollout, identify the failing candidate, then choose a tested revert or forward fix. Rewriting shared history as a surprise is ruled out.

foundation.question: notes.txt is modified, staged, then modified again. What does git status --short show?
options: MM notes.txt
M  notes.txt
M notes.txt
foundation.explanation: The first column is the index compared with HEAD and the second is the working tree compared with the index. Both differ, so both show M.

foundation.question: You run git commit --amend -m "Better message" on your latest, unpublished commit. What happens to its ID?
options: A new commit with a new ID replaces it on the branch, with the same parent
The ID stays the same because only the message changed
The commit gains a second parent
foundation.explanation: The message is part of the commit object, so amending creates a different commit. The branch moves to it; the old one stays reachable from the reflog for a while.

foundation.question: Which command prints the parent IDs of the current commit?
options: git log --pretty=%P -n 1
git diff --cached
git status --short
foundation.explanation: %P is the parent hashes placeholder. A normal commit has one parent and a merge commit has two.

intermediate.question: main and topic each change a different, distant line of the same file. What does git merge topic do?
options: Merges cleanly and creates a merge commit
Stops with a conflict in that file
Fast-forwards main to topic
intermediate.explanation: Git merges line ranges, not whole files. Separate, non-adjacent changes combine without a conflict. The branches diverged, so a merge commit records both.

intermediate.question: You run git revert on a merge commit without any options. What happens?
options: Git refuses until -m names the parent to keep
Git reverts both parents' changes
Git reverts the merge and deletes the topic branch
intermediate.explanation: A merge has two parents, so Git cannot tell which side's changes to undo. -m 1 keeps the first parent's history and reverts what the merge brought in.

intermediate.question: After git fetch, what does git log main..origin/main list?
options: Commits on origin/main that main does not have
Commits on main that origin/main does not have
Every commit on both branches
intermediate.explanation: A..B lists commits reachable from B but not from A. Here that is what fetching brought in and you have not integrated yet.

advanced.question: You run git tag v1.0 with no -a, -m or -s option. What does git cat-file -t v1.0 report?
options: commit: a lightweight tag points straight at the commit
tag: every tag creates a tag object
blob: tags store a file
advanced.explanation: Without -a, -m or -s, a tag is just a reference to a commit with no tag object, tagger or message. Annotated tags create a tag object.

advanced.question: During git bisect run, the test script exits with code 125 for one revision. How does Git treat that revision?
options: Skips it as untestable
Marks it bad
Stops the bisection with an error
advanced.explanation: 125 is reserved for revisions that cannot be tested. Git skips them and keeps searching, as the lesson recommends for unrelated build failures.

advanced.question: You cherry-pick a commit whose change is already on the current branch. What does Git do by default?
options: Stops and reports that the cherry-pick is empty
Creates a second commit with the same change
Removes the original commit from its branch
advanced.explanation: Applying the change produces no difference, so Git stops and asks whether to skip it or commit it with --allow-empty. Nothing is duplicated silently.
